beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Scientific Reproducibility Three: Containers. How to put a program and everything it needs into one file, run it on a cluster with Apptainer, and record it so someone else can repeat your results.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. To repeat a result, sharing your code is not enough. The libraries and the system under it change. A container seals the whole software stack into one file.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. Container: a sealed bundle of a program and what it needs. Image: the file a container is made from. Apptainer: runs containers on shared clusters. S I F file: Apptainer's single-file image. Bind: shows a folder from the machine inside the container. And tag: the version label on an image.

beats.narration_text: A container is one sealed file. Inside it sit a program, its libraries, its settings, and a small runtime. Move that file to a laptop, to a cluster, or to the cloud, and what is inside does not change.

The sealed box slides in turn onto a laptop slab, a cluster rack and a cloud, and is the same box with the same four labels visible on a tag each time.

beats.narration_text: You will meet three names. Docker is the most common tool, on laptops, cloud servers, and most published images. Singularity is the older name of the cluster tool. Apptainer is its current name, and it is what Northeastern's clusters, Explorer and AICR, use.

beats.narration_text: Why not use Docker on a cluster? Docker's normal setup needs administrator-level power, and on a machine shared by thousands of people that is a security problem. Apptainer runs the container as you, with your permissions and no more. It can still read Docker images.

shot.visual_intent: A cluster rack in the middle with many small plain dots around it (the other users). Left: the Docker logo chip holds a large kraft key labelled 'admin' that reaches into the rack; a cross lands on it. Right: Professor Bear portrait beside the Apptainer logo chip; a small arrow 'as you' enters the rack with one small key; a thin arrow from a Docker logo image block 'image' into the Apptainer chip shows it reads Docker images; a terracotta check.

beats.narration_text: First benefit: reproducible. The whole software stack is captured, so your result ties to one named, versioned image. A collaborator running it six months from now gets the same software, even after the system underneath has been updated.

beats.narration_text: Portable: the same file runs on your laptop, on Explorer, on another cluster, or in the cloud. And no dependency fights. Two tools that need incompatible versions of one library each get their own image, so neither one breaks the other.

beats.narration_text: Shareable: it is one file you can hand to a collaborator, archive with your data, or point a reviewer at. And ready-made: registries such as Docker Hub, Key dot I O, NVIDIA's N G C, and BioContainers host thousands of maintained images.

beats.narration_text: Containers cost something: images are large, and the first build takes effort. So try a module first, software the cluster already installed. Then conda, a package manager. Then a container, when the install is painful or you need a portable record.

A small figure token is NOT used; a terracotta ring marks the step you take only when the previous one fails; an arrow climbs the steps on the spoken words, and a weight label 'large images' sits on the top step.

beats.narration_text: Apptainer has three verbs. Exec runs one command inside the container, then returns. That is the verb for jobs. Shell opens an interactive shell inside it, for poking around and testing. And run does the container's built-in default action.

beats.narration_text: Run containers on a compute node, never on the login node. The login node is shared by everyone, and heavy work there gets terminated. Ask Slurm for a compute node first with S run, then work inside that session.

beats.narration_text: Then open a shell in an image. The path is a placeholder for your own project. Your prompt changes to Apptainer, which tells you that you are inside. Type exit to leave. Inside, you have only what the image holds, plus the folders you bind in.

beats.narration_text: On a GPU, the container can carry its own CUDA, so you do not match the node's modules. But it still needs the node's driver. The dash dash N V flag passes that driver in. Without it, the container has no link to the GPU.

beats.narration_text: The bind flag takes a folder on the host, a colon, and the path where it appears inside. Binding the same path on both sides is the simplest habit, because your script's paths then mean the same inside and out. Use absolute paths, and bind only what the job needs.

beats.narration_text: Always pin the tag. A tag called latest points at a different image next month. A pinned tag keeps pointing at the same one. So never use latest for anything you must reproduce, and write the exact tag into your methods.

beats.narration_text: Keep images in your project's containers folder, not in home. Project space is shared with your lab, and is not covered by the seventy-five gigabyte home quota. Keep the recipe next to the image, commit it, and archive the image with your data.

beats.act: VII · Habits That Keep It Honest
beats.narration_text: Apptainer keeps pulled layers in a hidden folder in your home directory, and a big pull can fill your quota, after which your OnDemand sessions stop working. Point both locations at project space before any large pull. The cache is only a cache.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A container is one sealed file holding a program and everything it needs. Apptainer runs it as you, so it fits a shared cluster. Run on a compute node with exec, shell or run, add the N V flag for a GPU, and bind every folder the job needs. Build where you have root, never on the cluster, then copy the finished file in. Pull on a compute node, pin the tag, and keep the recipe beside the image. And record the image, and say plainly what you tested and what you only read.
